title: Massive performance degradation for complex query on PostgreSQL 16+
body: I maintain Indico and found that a statistics query which takes only a few seconds on PostgreSQL 14/15 can take more than three hours on PostgreSQL 16.11, with massive CPU and disk usage. The supplied container reproducer behaves well on 14, and on 15 with increased shared memory, but becomes impractical on 16 through 18. I shared the SQL data set, the query, and EXPLAIN ANALYZE outputs from PostgreSQL 14 and 16.

symptoms_visible: The statistics query finishes in a few seconds on PostgreSQL 14/15 but took more than three hours on our PostgreSQL 16.11 production database.
On the supplied PostgreSQL 16 through 18 reproducer, CPU and disk usage grow rapidly into tens of gigabytes, so I stop the query rather than wait for it.
N0.label: N0 severe version-dependent slowdown reported

symptoms_visible: With work_mem set to 128MB, the query finishes normally on PostgreSQL 16 and 18.
The PostgreSQL 18 run with work_mem at 128MB also completes when enable_memoize is set to off.
N1.label: N1 memory and memoize probes completed

symptoms_visible: Using the updated larger data set, PostgreSQL 14 remains fast.
On PostgreSQL 16 with 4MB work_mem, CPU and disk usage explode and I abort after a few seconds; with 32MB, the query completes.
N2.label: N2 data mismatch controlled and regression retained

symptoms_visible: With parallel query enabled, the reproducer takes about 1.4 seconds on PostgreSQL 15 but about 160 seconds on PostgreSQL 16 through 18.
With parallel query disabled, all tested versions finish in roughly 3.5 to 4 seconds.
A PostgreSQL 16 run increases the counters by about two million temporary files and roughly 70GB, and its temporary directory grows to tens of gigabytes.
The instrumented run repeatedly initializes more batches until it reaches 262144.
N3.label: N3 parallel hash and temporary-file explosion measured

symptoms_visible: The git-bisected build starts showing the same temporary-file explosion at commit 11c2d6fdf5af1aacec9ca2005543f1b0fc4cc364, whose subject is 'Parallel Hash Full Join'.
I can reduce the reproducer to one LEFT OUTER JOIN by forcing a parallel hash join; it still exhibits the failure.
One run ends with 'ERROR: invalid DSA memory alloc request size 1811939328' in a parallel worker while retaining the same temporary-file explosion.
N4.label: N4 first bad build and minimal join isolated

symptoms_visible: The original simplified query no longer fails on current master.
After reverting commit 1811f1af98fb237fdd5adb588cd4b57c433b75f8, the original simplified query fails again.
Alternative query variants with IS NOT NULL continue to run successfully even after that revert.
N5.label: N5 null-key handling fix experimentally verified

symptoms_visible: On a PostgreSQL build containing the null-join-key hash-join fix, the supplied query completes without runaway batch growth, millions of temporary files, or tens of gigabytes of temporary disk usage.
N_terminal.label: terminal resolved

question_patterns: Can you rerun the query on PostgreSQL 16 and 18 with work_mem increased to 128MB?
Does a larger work_mem prevent the hash-join batching slowdown?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: I tried work_mem=128MB, and the query worked fine on both PostgreSQL 16 and PostgreSQL 18. I shared the EXPLAIN ANALYZE results for both runs.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: The query still takes hours and creates tens of gigabytes of temporary data with work_mem set to 128MB.
The query also completes at 96MB, with a similar plan and runtime.

question_patterns: What plan and runtime do you get with enable_memoize set to off?
Can you test SET enable_memoize = 0 and share the resulting plan?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: I also ran PostgreSQL 18 with work_mem=128MB and enable_memoize=0, and shared the resulting plan at https://explain.depesz.com/s/SaVI.

edges.comment: The larger-work_mem and memoize runs are handler-initiated configuration probes. The larger memory setting is a viable operational workaround, but these runs do not by themselves identify the executor defect.

question_patterns: Can you repeat the comparison using the same, current data set on both PostgreSQL versions?
The earlier plans have different row counts; does the regression remain when both versions use the same data copy?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: Good catch: my first test data came from an older production copy. I regenerated a larger current data set and replaced the SQL file. With that same data, PostgreSQL 14 is still fine and PostgreSQL 16 still has the severe slowdown at low work_mem.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: Once I use the same current data set, PostgreSQL 14 and 16 have comparable runtimes and disk usage.

question_patterns: What happens on the updated data set at the default 4MB work_mem and at 32MB?
Can you compare PostgreSQL 16 with low and moderately increased work_mem?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: On PostgreSQL 16 at 4MB, CPU and disk usage became massive, so I aborted after a few seconds. At 32MB it completed, and I shared the EXPLAIN ANALYZE output.

edges.comment: This controls for the row-count discrepancy between the original production plans. The same-copy result rules out different data snapshots as the explanation for the version regression.

question_patterns: Can you reproduce the query across PostgreSQL 14 through 18 with parallel query enabled and report the timings?
Which PostgreSQL release first becomes slow under the same parallel plan conditions?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: I reproduced it with the supplied scripts. My timings were 1551.363ms on 14, 1385.414ms on 15, 161571.400ms on 16, 156434.543ms on 17, and 159095.001ms on 18.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: The timings are approximately 1.5 seconds on every version from PostgreSQL 14 through 18 with parallel query enabled.
PostgreSQL 16 through 18 take around 145 seconds rather than around 160 seconds, while 14 and 15 remain near 1.5 seconds.

question_patterns: What happens if you disable parallel query and repeat the version comparison?
Does the regression remain in a non-parallel plan?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: With parallel query disabled, I got 3990.439ms on 14, 3518.453ms on 15, 3606.460ms on 16, 3591.039ms on 17, and 3617.872ms on 18.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: Disabling parallel query makes no difference: PostgreSQL 16 through 18 are still about one hundred times slower.

question_patterns: Can you compare pg_stat_database temp_files and temp_bytes before and after the query?
How much temporary-file activity does PostgreSQL 16 produce compared with PostgreSQL 15?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: Both runs began at 112 temp files and 1942275280 temp bytes. PostgreSQL 15 ended at 721 files and 2755839184 bytes, while PostgreSQL 16 ended at 2078995 files and 70607906000 bytes. During the run, one fileset directory reached about 63GB.

question_patterns: Can you instrument parallel hash batch setup and report the batch counts it initializes?
Does the problematic hash join repeatedly increase its number of batches?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: With a warning added to ExecParallelHashJoinSetUpBatches, I saw it repeatedly initialize larger counts: 128, 256, 512, and so on, ending at 131072 and 262144 batches.

edges.comment: These measurements came from an independent developer reproducing the reporter's supplied scripts; that reproducer is folded into the simulated user side. The raw timings, counters, and warning output establish that the regression requires parallel execution and involves explosive hash batching.

question_patterns: Can you git-bisect PostgreSQL between the working and failing revisions?
What is the first bad commit from a source-level bisection?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: I bisected with the full query. The first failing revision was 11c2d6fdf5af1aacec9ca2005543f1b0fc4cc364, dated March 31, 2023, with the subject 'Parallel Hash Full Join'.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: The bisection's first bad revision is an unrelated planner selectivity change, before any parallel hash outer-join work.
The same first bad commit is found after minimizing the query before running the bisection.

question_patterns: Can you minimize the query while preserving the failure?
Does the issue remain with a single join if planner costs are adjusted to force a parallel hash join?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: I reduced it to a single LEFT OUTER JOIN between attachments.folders and events.contributions. With parallel_setup_cost=0, cpu_tuple_cost=1, and enable_nestloop=off, it still reproduces the problem.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: The issue disappears as soon as any one join is removed, and I cannot reproduce it outside the full seven-table query.

question_patterns: Does the minimized or bisected run finish, or does it report an error?
What is the exact error from the failing parallel worker?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: One run ended with 'ERROR: invalid DSA memory alloc request size 1811939328' and 'CONTEXT: parallel worker'. I still saw the same temporary-file explosion.

question_patterns: What does the join-key data look like — how many NULL contribution_id rows are there, and does filtering them out change the hang?
Could you run the reproducer with WHERE contribution_id IS NOT NULL and report what happens?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: folders.contribution_id has about 464,515 NULL rows (contributions.id is unique — it's the PK); adding WHERE contribution_id IS NOT NULL makes the join complete in about 670ms, while inverting the condition to IS NULL starts failing pretty much right away.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: There are zero NULL contribution_id rows; the IS NOT NULL filter changes nothing.

edges.comment: The bisection answer contains the commit printed by the raw git-bisect result. Explaining why that change affects a query containing a LEFT JOIN rather than a FULL JOIN remains engineer-side inference.

question_patterns: Does current master still fail, and what happens if you revert commit 1811f1af98fb237fdd5adb588cd4b57c433b75f8?
Can you test whether the recent null-join-key hash-join change fixes the original simplified query?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: With the original simplified query, I get no failures on current master. It starts failing again after I revert 1811f1af98fb237fdd5adb588cd4b57c433b75f8.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: Current master still has the same temporary-file explosion, and reverting 1811f1af makes no difference.
Current master succeeds and the failure returns after reverting the same commit, but the exact runtime varies between runs.

edges.comment: This is a requested try/revert measurement. The independent reproducer also volunteered that IS NOT NULL variants remained successful after the revert, further distinguishing the null-key-sensitive failing case.

solution.intent: Use a PostgreSQL build containing commit 1811f1af98fb237fdd5adb588cd4b57c433b75f8, which corrects hash join handling of tuples with null join keys and prevents the parallel hash join from exploding to hundreds of thousands of batches.
solution.concrete_example: Apply or update to a PostgreSQL build containing 1811f1af98fb237fdd5adb588cd4b57c433b75f8 ('Improve hash join's handling of tuples with null join keys'). Keep increased work_mem or disabled parallel query only as temporary mitigations until the fixed build is available.
solution.inference_hint: The reporter and reproducer supplied raw evidence: the version boundary, parallel-only behavior, millions of temporary files, growth to 262144 batches, the first bad 11c2d6 revision, and the current-master/revert result for 1811f1af. Concluding that null-key tuples prevented the parallel hash join's stop-partitioning logic from terminating futile repartitioning is engineer analysis derived from those measurements.

edges.comment: The technical resolution is the null-join-key hash-join correction verified by the current-master and revert test. Questions about which supported release branches receive the change are release coordination and are deliberately not scored.

satisfaction_conditions: Must identify the root cause as a PostgreSQL 16-era parallel hash join regression involving tuples with null join keys: futile repartitioning grows the join to hundreds of thousands of batches and creates millions of temporary files and tens of gigabytes of temporary data.

The diagnosis must be grounded in the collected evidence: the same-data version comparison, disappearance of the regression when parallel query is disabled, temporary-file counters, 262144-batch instrumentation, the minimized LEFT JOIN, the 11c2d6 bisection output, and the 1811f1af revert test.

Must recommend a PostgreSQL build containing commit 1811f1af98fb237fdd5adb588cd4b57c433b75f8 or its equivalent null-join-key hash-join fix; larger work_mem or disabling parallel query may be offered only as temporary mitigations.

Must not attribute the root cause to Memoize or to the original data-snapshot mismatch: Memoize was not determinative, and the regression remained after repeating the comparison with the same updated data.

Must not declare resolution from the workaround alone; the fixed code path must be verified with the supplied reproducer, as demonstrated by current master succeeding and the failure returning when 1811f1af is reverted.

persona_hint.experience_level: Highly technical application maintainer comfortable operating multiple PostgreSQL versions in containers, sharing large SQL reproducers and EXPLAIN ANALYZE plans, changing server settings, and comparing production-like data sets. Independent PostgreSQL developers contribute source instrumentation, benchmarks, query minimization, and git-bisect results and are folded into the simulated user side.
persona_hint.communication_style: Detailed, cooperative, and evidence-driven. Reports exact settings and links, corrects test-data mistakes promptly, distinguishes a useful workaround from a real fix, and asks concise practical follow-ups.
